f: In March 2012 Greece swapped its privately held bonds at a loss of more than half their face value: the biggest sovereign restructuring in history.
In November 2011 Italy's 10-year yield averaged 7.06%. Silvio Berlusconi resigned as prime minister that same month.
Spain's 10-year yield averaged 6.79% in July 2012, the month Mario Draghi promised to do "whatever it takes" to save the euro.
Portugal asked for an EU-IMF bailout in April 2011. Its 10-year yield peaked at 13.85% in January 2012.
Ireland's banking collapse ended in an €85bn EU-IMF rescue in November 2010. Its yield peaked at 12.45% in July 2011.
Paul Volcker's Fed squeezed out inflation with record interest rates. The 10-year Treasury averaged 15.32% in September 1981, its all-time high.
On 16 September 1992, "Black Wednesday", the pound crashed out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism.
In September 1992 Sweden's central bank raised its overnight rate to 500% to defend the krona. It let the currency float two months later.
In September 1992 the lira was forced out of the European Exchange Rate Mechanism, the same week as the pound.
The Fed's surprise hikes in 1994 caused the "great bond massacre": the 10-year Treasury went from 5.75% in January to 7.96% in November.
The Bank of Japan announced negative interest rates in January 2016, effective in February. That month Japan's 10-year yield averaged below zero for the first time.
Japan's asset bubble burst in 1990. Its 10-year yield peaked at 8.03% in September 1990, then began a decades-long slide.
In January 2015 the Swiss National Bank scrapped its cap on the franc. Swiss 10-year yields were negative in 59 of the 72 months from 2015 to 2020.
Germany's 10-year yield first averaged below zero in June 2016, the month of the Brexit vote.
The September 2022 "mini-budget" set off a gilt sell-off: the 10-year yield jumped from 2.33% in August to 3.50% in September, and the Bank of England stepped in.
In March 2020 the 10-year Treasury averaged below 1% for the first time, at 0.87%.
In October 2023 the 10-year Treasury averaged 4.80%, its highest monthly level since July 2007.
After François Mitterrand won the presidency in May 1981, capital fled France and its 10-year yield passed 17%.
A currency crisis after New Zealand's 1984 snap election led to sweeping free-market reforms. Its yield peaked at 18.71% in May 1985.
In September 1985 South Africa froze repayments on its foreign debt after banks pulled their credit lines.
The 1998 emerging-market crisis hit the rand hard. South Africa's 10-year yield averaged 18.30% in September 1998.
Canadian rates followed the Fed up. Canada's 10-year yield peaked at 17.00% in September 1981.
Hungarian inflation passed 25% in early 2023, among the highest in the EU. Its 10-year yield peaked at 10.25% in October 2022.
Poland joined the EU in 2004. Its 10-year yield fell from 11.86% in August 2001 to 4.72% in July 2005.
Greece adopted the euro in January 2001. By mid-2003 its 10-year yield was within 0.2 points of Germany's.
Italy's 10-year yield fell from 13.45% in March 1995 to below 5% by July 1998 as it raced to qualify for the euro.
In 1976 Britain borrowed $3.9bn from the IMF, then the largest loan the fund had ever made.
Ireland's 1980s debt crisis pushed its 10-year yield to 19.47% in February 1982.
Oil prices collapsed in 1986 and hit Norway hard: the krone was devalued by 12% in May 1986.
A banking crisis and the collapse of Soviet trade sank Finland's economy in 1991. The markka was floated in September 1992.
During the second intifada and a sliding shekel, Israel's 10-year yield reached 11.67% in October 2002. It peaked at 11.69% in February 2003.
The 2008 financial crisis pushed Mexico's 10-year yield to 9.82% in November 2008.
Chile's 2019 protests were followed by pension-fund withdrawals. Its 10-year yield rose from 2.70% in August 2019 to 6.34% in October 2021.
South Korea's 10-year yield fell to 1.25% in August 2019, then climbed to 4.27% in October 2022.
Slovenia's yield peaked at 6.90% in December 2011. In 2013 it rescued its own banks and narrowly avoided an EU bailout.
Australia floated its dollar in December 1983, ending decades of a managed exchange rate.
Inflation rose with the Vietnam War. In August 1971 Richard Nixon ended the dollar's convertibility into gold.
The 1973 oil shock pushed German 10-year yields above 10% in 1974, peaking at 10.8%.
Money poured into the franc in the late 1970s. In October 1978 the Swiss National Bank set a floor against the Deutsche Mark.
Spain devalued the peseta three times between September 1992 and May 1993.
Belgium's public debt passed 100% of GDP in the 1980s, one of the highest levels in Europe.
Until the 1980s Norway's interest rates were set by the authorities, not the market, and bank credit was rationed by quotas. That is why the line moves in steps.
Norway's government bond yield hit 13.7% in 1982, the highest level in a record going back to 1819.
In autumn 1982 Denmark fixed its exchange rate, banned wage indexation and tightened its budget. Long-term yields fell from 22.93% in June 1982 to 14.19% by April 1983.
In 1981 the Bank of Italy stopped having to buy the government bonds the Treasury could not sell, the so-called divorce. From then on the market set the price.
From 1976 Austria tied the schilling to the Deutsche Mark, its hard-currency policy. It held until the euro replaced both.
In the 1970s Switzerland tried to stop money flooding into the franc by charging foreigners negative interest on their deposits. The franc kept rising anyway.
On 1 September 1998 Malaysia imposed capital controls and pegged the ringgit at 3.80 to the dollar, rather than turn to the IMF.
In December 2008 Latvia agreed a €7.5 billion rescue from the EU, the IMF, its Nordic neighbours and others. Its economy shrank by about 14% in 2009.
In March 2009 Romania secured a €20 billion rescue package from the IMF and the EU.
Bulgaria adopted the euro on 1 January 2026, becoming the 21st member of the euro area.
Croatia adopted the euro in January 2023, replacing the kuna.
In 1987 Japan's 10-year yield jumped from 3.78% in May to 6.10% in October, a bond-market rout in the middle of the bubble years.
In October 2008 Iceland's three biggest banks collapsed within a week.
Cyprus's March 2013 bailout made large bank depositors take losses, a first for the euro area.
In February 2015 Sweden's central bank cut its main rate below zero, to -0.1%.
In July 2012 Denmark's central bank became one of the first in the world to set a negative interest rate.
